attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. He is doing the calculation himself, not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: Keeps the assumption that AWS and Google spend is comparable, keeps the firm 'most-assuredly more', and supplies the omitted monthly unit for $3.75B. The context makes this a run-rate estimate starting in July, which was still in the future when he wrote. Observation is acceptable for a spending-level calculation.

contract.note: Anchoring the claim to the July rate follows from the sentence before it. Reading $3.75B as monthly is the ordinary reading. The contract rightly treats the correct arithmetic and the firm 'more' assertion as separate commitments. No numerical tolerance is given.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own announcement confirms the SpaceX capacity deal. It gives no July charges for SpaceX, AWS or Google.

Revenue per compute dollar in this report implies about $9.9B of Q3 compute spend, below the $11.25B quarterly figure. But it covers a different period (all of Q3, not July), provider coverage and accounting basis are unclear, and it is relayed from unnamed sources. It is strong countercontext but not decisive.

reviews.rationale: No July charges by provider were found, so neither the assumption that AWS and Google spend is comparable nor the firm claim that spending is 'more' can be checked. The implied Q3 compute total of about $9.9B points against the claim, but its period, scope and basis do not match. The evidence available by the cutoff does not settle the outcome.

semantics.note: The proposition captures the core allegation: a preferential deal that artificially lowered costs. It leaves out that Amodei and Musk personally arranged it, but nothing scored depends on that.

contract.note: The contract fairly separates the narrow fact (lower fees in May and June) from the stronger allegation (preferential pricing that artificially lowered costs). Neither 'sweetheart' nor 'artificially' comes with a benchmark, so interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: Reports the filing's term that fees were reduced during the May–June ramp-up. That supports only the narrow lower-fee part, not below-market pricing or artificial cost suppression.
Company announcement saying capacity would arrive 'within the month'. It neither proves nor rules out an ordinary ramp-up explanation for the lower fees.

reviews.rationale: The evidence confirms that fees were lower in May and June. Nothing in the packet shows what capacity was actually delivered, what comparable prices were, or how the reduction was booked, so it cannot show the reduction was preferential or 'artificial' rather than an ordinary ramp-up. The core causal allegation is neither established nor refuted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his own post.

semantics.note: Reading 'that's not what's happening' as a rejection of the profit report as proof is a fair reading. The claim is largely interpretive: it bundles operating profit, profitable inference and business-model viability together.

contract.note: The contract tests the claim as whether the reported profit reflects lasting underlying economics once temporary pricing effects and excluded costs are counted. That fits the context and is an ordinary reading, but the result depends on it.

evidence.note: Shows the projected Q2 profit excluded stock-based compensation. That supports only the narrow point that the profit measure was adjusted.

The prospectus, as reported, shows GAAP Q2 operating income of $974M, so the profit survives the expenses that projection left out. It does not separate out the SpaceX discount, show whether inference itself is profitable, or show that profitability lasts.

reviews.rationale: The GAAP figure (e2) shows positive Q2 operating income even with stock compensation included, which weakens the claim that the profit came only from leaving costs out. But no evidence puts a number on the temporary SpaceX discount or isolates inference profitability, and those are what the contract's support and contradiction tests require. The outcome is not settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will continue ... in perpetuity' is an unqualified forecast with no finite horizon. Scope as AI labs matches the context. The present-tense part of the claim is folded into the forecast.

contract.note: Reading 'linearly' as roughly proportional cost growth is ordinary and fair. 'Costs' and the accounting basis are undefined, so interpretation decides the result. The contract rightly allows only an adverse early resolution.

evidence.note: Anthropic's prospectus shows operating expenses falling as a share of revenue up to Q2 2026, which is countercontext. Only Q2 overlaps the period after publication, and that quarter is the discounted one the post disputes. It is not a sustained departure after publication.

reviews.rationale: The forecast runs forever, so it has no deadline. The early-resolution rule needs a sustained departure from proportional cost growth after publication, on a consistent basis. The only overlapping evidence is one disputed, discounted quarter, so that rule is not met. The pre-publication trend runs against the claim but is context only. The forecast stays open and unscored.
